Cell-type-specific exposure dose-response analysis

Source: R/dose-response.R
run_dose_response.Rd

Fits linear and polynomial dose-response models for each gene within a cell type, testing whether the exposure-expression relationship is nonlinear. Linear exposure-response models are common, but some exposures, such as endocrine-disrupting chemicals, show non-monotonic dose responses (Vandenberg et al. 2012).

Usage

run_dose_response(
  x,
  exposure,
  celltype,
  celltype_col = "cell_type",
  target_genes = NULL,
  max_degree = 3L,
  min_cells = 10L
)

Arguments

x

A SingleCellExposomeExperiment. Each cell's donor is read from the colData column named by sampleColumn(x).

exposure

Character. Exposure variable name.

celltype

Character. Target cell type.

celltype_col

Character. colData column with cell type labels. Default "cell_type".

target_genes

Character vector (optional). Genes to test. Default: top 50 most variable genes.

max_degree

Integer. Maximum polynomial degree to test. Default 3 (cubic). Higher values risk overfitting with small sample sizes.

min_cells

Integer. Minimum cells per donor. Default 10.

Value

A DataFrame with columns: gene, best_model ("linear", "quadratic", "cubic"), linear_coef, AIC_linear, AIC_best, p_nonlinear (F-test of nonlinear_model against the linear model), nonlinear_model, celltype, n_donors (donors with at least min_cells cells and a non-missing exposure; donors with a missing exposure are left out, with a message).

Details

For each gene, the function fits:

  1. y ~ exposure (linear)

  2. y ~ poly(exposure, 2) (quadratic)

  3. y ~ poly(exposure, 3) (cubic, if max_degree >= 3)

on pseudobulk log-CPM values. best_model is the model with the lowest AIC and is descriptive.

p_nonlinear is an F-test of the highest-degree polynomial that could be fitted (cubic when max_degree = 3 and at least six donors are available, otherwise quadratic) against the linear model. It is fixed in advance and does not depend on the AIC selection, because testing the model chosen by AIC would overstate the evidence for nonlinearity.

References

Vandenberg LN et al. (2012). Hormones and endocrine- disrupting chemicals: low-dose effects and nonmonotonic dose responses. Endocr Rev 33:378-455. doi:10.1210/er.2011-1050

Examples

library(SingleCellExperiment); library(S4Vectors)
set.seed(1)
counts <- matrix(rpois(5000, 8), nrow = 50,
    dimnames = list(paste0("G", 1:50), paste0("c", 1:100)))
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts),
    colData = DataFrame(cell_id = paste0("c", 1:100),
        donor_id = rep(paste0("D", 1:10), each = 10),
        cell_type = rep(c("Mono", "NK"), 50)))
exp_mat <- matrix(rnorm(20), nrow = 10,
    dimnames = list(paste0("D", 1:10), c("E1", "E2")))
scee <- build_scee(sce, exp_mat, sample_col = "donor_id")
dr <- run_dose_response(scee, exposure = "E1",
    celltype = "Mono", celltype_col = "cell_type",
    min_cells = 3L,
    max_degree = 2L)
head(dr)
